Aims To determine the relationship between PTX3 systemic and synovial levels and the clinical features of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in a cohort of early, treatment naïve patients and to explore the relevance of PTX3 expression in predicting response to conventional-synthetic (cs) Disease-Modifying-Anti-Rheumatic-Drugs (DMARDs) treatment. Methods PTX3 expression was analyzed in 119 baseline serum samples from early naïve RA patients, 95 paired samples obtained 6-months following the initiation of cs-DMARDs treatment and 43 healthy donors. RNA-sequencing analysis and immunohistochemistry for PTX3 were performed on a subpopulation of 79 and 58 synovial samples, respectively, to assess PTX3 gene and protein expression. Immunofluorescence staining was performed to characterize PTX3 expressing cells within the synovium. Results Circulating levels of PTX3 were significantly higher in early RA compared to healthy donors and correlated with disease activity at baseline and with the degree of structural damages at 12-months. Six-months after commencing cs-DMARDs, a high level of PTX3, proportional to the baseline value, was still detectable in the serum of patients, regardless of their response status. RNA-seq analysis confirmed that synovial transcript levels of PTX3 correlated with disease activity and the presence of mediators of inflammation, tissue remodeling and bone destruction at baseline. PTX3 expression in the synovium was strongly linked to the degree of immune cell infiltration, the presence of ectopic lymphoid structures and seropositivity for autoantibodies. Accordingly, PTX3 was found to be expressed by numerous synovial cell types such as plasma cells, fibroblasts, vascular and lymphatic endothelial cells, macrophages, and neutrophils. The percentage of PTX3-positive synovial cells, although significantly reduced at 6-months post-treatment as a result of global decreased cellularity, was similar in cs-DMARDs responders and non-responders. Conclusion This study demonstrates that, early in the disease and prior to treatment modification, the level of circulating PTX3 is a reliable marker of RA activity and predicts a high degree of structural damages at 12-months. In the joint, PTX3 associates with immune cell infiltration and the presence of ectopic lymphoid structures. High synovial and peripheral blood levels of PTX3 are associated with chronic inflammation characteristic of RA. Additional studies to determine the mechanistic link are required. pentraxin-3 rheumatoid arthritis synovial tissue pathotypes inflammation Introduction Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most common chronic inflammatory autoimmune joint disease. It is characterized by synovitis and progressive cartilage destruction and bone erosions, and can lead to persistent joint pain and functional disability. Defective control of the systemic inflammatory response and the development of autoimmunity, often emerging long before the clinical onset of the disease, result in the synovial infiltration and activation of immune and stromal cells that lead to the production of high levels of inflammatory mediators such as pro-inflammatory interleukins (IL-1, Tumor Necrosis Factor-TNF-α, IL-6) or matrix metalloproteinases (MMP) ( 1 ). These molecules contribute to the maintenance of synovitis, which displays histopathological variability that has been categorized into three partially overlapping pathotypes ( 2 ). These include the lympho-myeloid pathotype characterized by the presence of B/T cells forming organized ectopic lymphoid structures (ELS), plasma cells and macrophages; the diffuse-myeloid pathotype with a predominant infiltration of macrophages without organized ELS, and the pauci-immune fibroid pathotype defined by a scant immune cell infiltrate. These pathotypes have been shown to stratify disease activity and severity, as well as response to conventional synthetic (cs) disease modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARDs) ( 3 ). Furthermore, soluble proteins such as the classical short pentraxin C-reactive protein (CRP), in addition to acting as acute phase reactants and indicator of systemic inflammation, also reflect joint disease activity and tissue pathology ( 3 , 4 ). The long pentraxin 3 (PTX3) is a soluble pattern recognition molecule highly conserved in evolution ( 5 ). PTX3 is generally poorly expressed in homeostatic conditions, but is rapidly upregulated in response to inflammatory stimuli. For instance, the proinflammatory molecules IL-1 and TNF are the most important inducers of PTX3 production by myeloid and endothelial cells. When appropriately stimulated, fibroblasts and other stromal cells also release PTX3. PTX3 is a multifunctional protein exerting non-redundant roles in the innate resistance to pathogens, the regulation of inflammation and tissue repair. It has been shown that PTX3 can limit tissue damage in murine models of acute lung injury and ischemia/reperfusion-induced kidney injury by regulating neutrophil recruitment at inflamed sites ( 6 , 7 ). In experimental models of chemically-induced sterile liver and lung injury, skin wound healing and in arterial thrombosis, PTX3-deficiency is associated with altered remodeling of the fibrin-rich inflammatory matrix and impairment of normal tissue repair ( 8 ). Similarly to CRP, PTX3 circulating levels are increased in several inflammatory or infectious pathological conditions and are associated with disease severity and mortality risk ( 9 – 11 ). In the context of RA, PTX3 has been shown to be constitutively highly expressed by synovial fibroblasts ( 12 ); however, as described in other tissues, various resident or infiltrating synovial cells like macrophages or endothelial cells might also represent a source of PTX3 upon inflammatory activation. Several groups found that PTX3 is upregulated in the serum of RA patients compared to healthy donors ( 13 – 15 ) or patients with osteoarthritis ( 16 ). However, conflicting results have been published regarding the relationship between the level of PTX3 in the serum and clinical features of the disease. On the one hand, studies on different cohorts of 111 ( 17 ), 29 ( 18 ), 60 ( 13 ), 83 ( 19 ), 58 ( 14 ) or 41 ( 15 ) RA patients reported no relationship between PTX3 and the Disease Activity Score (DAS)-28. Conversely, other groups found an association between PTX3 serum levels and either CRP ( 16 ) or the progression of joint damage assessed by increase in the total van der Heijde modified Sharp score (SHSS) and joint space narrowing over 3 years ( 20 ). In addition, Weitoft and colleagues reported that the level of PTX3 in synovial fluid from RA patients is higher in seropositive patients (anti-cyclic citrullinated protein -CCP- antibody or rheumatoid factor -RF-) when compared to seronegative patients, and correlates with disease activity and local expression of markers of inflammation such as IL-6 or vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ( 21 ). These contradictory results likely depend on the heterogeneity of the cohorts analyzed including, for example, diverse disease stages, treatment exposure (cs- or biologic-DMARDs, known to influence various biologic processes), and disease phases (acute flare/latent chronic). For example, during acute flares, a dysregulated production of synovial fluid with a predominant infiltration of neutrophils will significantly influence PTX3 level. Here, to clarify the relationship between PTX3 systemic and synovial levels and clinical parameters while minimizing population heterogeneity and drug-exposure, we investigated a large cohort of treatment-naïve early RA patients. We performed a thorough analysis of PTX3 circulating and transcript/protein synovial expression at baseline and 6-months after cs-DMARDs exposure in matched individuals. Here, we provide important insights into the relevance of PTX3 in RA disease tissue pathology, disease severity and whether it is a useful biomarker predictive of treatment response in RA.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Early, treatment-naïve RA patients at baseline vs. healthy donors; onset of RA prior to any treatment; in RA patients with cs-DMARD treatment (6-months post-treatment).
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Significantly higher (vs. healthy), positively correlated (with disease activity markers and bone erosions), not reduced (post-treatment).
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Circulating PTX3 levels are significantly higher in early RA patients compared to healthy donors (e.g., RA median 3.23 ng/mL vs healthy median 1.25 ng/mL). At baseline, serum PTX3 positively correlated with disease activity markers (CRP, ESR, DAS28, tender/swollen joints, VAS physician assessment, HAQ) and with the degree of bone erosions (SHSS) at 12-months. After 6 months of cs-DMARD treatment, circulating PTX3 levels were not reduced, remaining high and proportional to baseline values, independent of clinical activity or erosion status. The correlation with most clinical parameters (except CRP) was lost at 6 months post-treatment.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: RA synovial tissue (baseline and post-treatment), specific synovial pathotypes (lympho-myeloid, diffuse-myeloid, pauci-immune), seropositive vs. seronegative RA patients, correlation with inflammatory cell infiltration and Krenn score.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Strongly correlated (with disease activity and inflammation mediators), negatively correlated (with OPG), positively and significantly associated (with TNF signaling/cell death mediators), significantly upregulated/higher expression (in lympho-myeloid pathotype), significantly higher expression (in seropositive patients, with immune cell infiltration), significantly decreased/diminished (post cs-DMARD treatment), significantly associated with reduction (of inflammatory cell markers post-treatment).
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Synovial PTX3 mRNA levels strongly correlated with disease activity (ESR, CRP, DAS28) and gene expression of acute phase reactants (CRP, SAA), chemokines, cytokines, and mediators of tissue remodeling and bone resorption (MMP, RANK). A negative correlation was observed with osteoprotegerin (OPG/TNFSFR11B). Synovial PTX3 expression was positively associated with mediators of TNF signaling and cell death (BAK1, BID, LTB, LTBR) and with CXCL- and CCL- chemokines involved in ELS formation. PTX3 (mRNA and protein) was significantly upregulated and more expressed in lympho-myeloid and diffuse-myeloid pathotypes, particularly higher in lympho-myeloid compared to pauci-immune pathotypes. The percentage of PTX3-positive synovial cells was significantly higher in lympho-myeloid pathotypes, in RF/CCP seropositive patients, and strongly correlated with synovial infiltration of CD3+ T cells, CD20+ B cells, CD138+ plasma cells, CD68+ macrophages, and total Krenn score. Following cs-DMARD treatment, the percentage of synovial PTX3-positive cells significantly decreased (due to global decreased cellularity and reduced inflammatory cell infiltration), although the decrease was independent of patient response status. Synovial PTX3 levels were significantly associated with the reduction of semi-quantitative scores for inflammatory cell markers post-treatment.
Lympho-myeloid pathotype showed significantly more active disease with higher ESR, CRP, and DAS28 levels compared to other pathotypes.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) inflammation, bone remodeling, immune activation, and specific synovial tissue pathotypes.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: PTX3 is a multifunctional protein rapidly upregulated by inflammatory stimuli (e.g., IL-1, TNF-α) from myeloid, endothelial, fibroblast, and stromal cells. It plays roles in innate immunity, inflammation regulation, and tissue repair, serving as a biomarker for systemic and local RA inflammation and disease activity. Synovial PTX3 expression correlates with acute phase reactants, chemokines, cytokines, and mediators of tissue remodeling and bone resorption (MMP, RANK), and negatively with osteoclastogenesis inhibitor OPG. It is associated with TNF signaling, cell death pathways, and pro-inflammatory, immune activation, and antiviral IFN signature modules, linking to pathways like neutrophil-mediated immunity, cytokine signaling, and leukocyte migration. PTX3 protein is expressed by various synovial cells (plasma cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, macrophages, neutrophils), and its levels reflect immune cell infiltration, particularly in lympho-myeloid pathotypes with ectopic lymphoid structures and seropositivity for autoantibodies. High peripheral PTX3 levels may perpetuate systemic inflammation and promote disease flares. Its local synovial expression diminishes post-cs-DMARD treatment due to reduced cellularity, as cs-DMARDs impact the functions of PTX3-producing immune cells. PTX3 can be enhanced by SAA, bridge innate and adaptive immunity, and is implicated in IL-6-driven pyroptosis. It may also play a protective role in bone remodeling by inhibiting FGF-2 associated osteoclastogenesis and promoting osteoblastogenesis.
related_biomarkers: VAS physician assessment of global health

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: PTX3 levels are significantly higher in RA patients compared to healthy donors. At baseline, serum PTX3 levels positively correlated with clinical parameters of disease severity (CRP, ESR, DAS28, tender/swollen joints, VAS physician assessment, HAQ). However, 6 months after cs-DMARD treatment, circulating PTX3 levels were not reduced and remained high, proportional to baseline values, independent of baseline clinical activity, erosion status, patient response status (responders/non-responders), different cs-DMARD types, or steroid treatment. This indicates that serum PTX3 is not significantly affected by cs-DMARDs or other treatments in the long term. In contrast, local synovial PTX3 protein levels and the percentage of PTX3-positive synovial cells significantly decreased following cs-DMARD treatment due to reduced cellularity, although this reduction was independent of the patient's response status. Neither peripheral nor local baseline PTX3 levels were predictive of specific response status to cs-DMARDs.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: While circulating PTX3 levels are increased in various inflammatory or infectious conditions, they are specifically upregulated in the serum of RA patients compared to healthy donors and those with osteoarthritis. At baseline, elevated PTX3 correlates with multiple disease activity markers in early untreated RA. However, this correlation is largely lost at 6-months post-treatment, reducing its predictive specificity after therapy. Serum PTX3 levels did not differentiate distinct synovial pathotypes. In contrast, synovial PTX3 (transcript and protein) is significantly higher in the lympho-myeloid pathotype compared to diffuse-myeloid and pauci-immune pathotypes. Synovial PTX3-positive cells also show higher expression in RF/CCP seropositive patients compared to seronegative patients. The significant decrease in synovial PTX3 expression following cs-DMARD treatment was observed universally, independent of response status.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Early (<12 months of symptoms), treatment-naïve Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) patients (2010 ACR/EULAR criteria), age- and gender-matched healthy donors/volunteers. Also relevant to general RA patients and potentially patients with psoriatic arthritis and spondylarthritis.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Circulating PTX3 is a reliable biomarker for baseline RA disease activity and predicts the future degree of structural damages (e.g., bone erosions) at 12 months. Higher serum PTX3 levels are associated with active disease and increased inflammatory status in early untreated RA, positively correlating with markers like CRP, ESR, and DAS28. High peripheral PTX3 levels may perpetuate systemic inflammation and promote disease flares. Synovial PTX3 (mRNA and protein) is strongly associated with local disease activity, inflammation, and immune cell infiltration within the synovium, particularly in lympho-myeloid pathotypes and RF/CCP seropositive patients. Synovial PTX3 levels decrease after cs-DMARD treatment, reflecting reduced local inflammation. PTX3 expression has also been linked to RA comorbidities like vasculitis or coronary artery disease, anticipating increased risks. While PTX3 has shown a protective role in bone remodeling (inhibiting osteoclastogenesis) in experimental models, neither serum nor synovial PTX3 is suitable for monitoring treatment response to cs-DMARDs.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: PTX3 demonstrates diagnostic utility as a marker of baseline RA disease activity and severity, predicting future structural damages (bone erosions) and characterizing specific RA synovial pathotypes (especially lympho-myeloid) and seropositivity (RF/CCP). It indicates adverse risk due to its association with chronic inflammation, perpetuation of systemic inflammation, potential disease flares, radiographic damage, deleterious tissue infiltration, and comorbidities (e.g., vasculitis, coronary artery disease). However, it has limited utility for monitoring treatment response to cs-DMARDs or as a predictive biomarker for treatment outcome. A protective benefit in bone remodeling has been observed in experimental models, though its overall contribution is debated in human RA.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Circulating PTX3 is a reliable marker for assessing baseline RA disease activity and predicting future structural damages (bone erosions). The study's focus on early, treatment-naïve patients minimized heterogeneity, addressing past conflicting results. Quantification used a reliable in-house ELISA with a detection limit of 0.1 ng/mL and 8-10% inter-assay variability, with blinded technical duplicates. However, serum PTX3's correlation with most clinical parameters diminishes after 6 months of cs-DMARD treatment, and it is unaffected by treatment or response status, limiting its utility for monitoring treatment efficacy or predicting response. In contrast, synovial PTX3 strongly and consistently correlates with local inflammation, disease activity, and specific histopathological features (lympho-myeloid pathotype, immune cell infiltration), and significantly decreases with cs-DMARDs, establishing it as a reliable marker for local joint inflammation. Despite this, neither serum nor synovial PTX3 reliably predicts individual patient response to cs-DMARDs. A non-linear correlation between synovial PTX3 transcript and protein expression suggests potential local post-transcriptional regulation. PTX3 is also a relevant biomarker in sepsis.
